conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived.  
We’ll use a short tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**—just ten gentle questions about the past seven days.  
The goal isn’t to label you; it’s simply to see how we can best support you in this huge life transition. Everything you share stays between you and the clinical team, and we can pause or stop any time.  
Ready when you are—shall we begin?

1. Over the last week, when you’ve been able to laugh at something funny, how often did you feel like you could genuinely enjoy the moment?

Most of the time I can still laugh—like when my sister sent me that silly video of the cat chasing its tail—but it feels a little flatter than it used to. I’d say I enjoy it, just not quite as brightly as before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh—like, my partner made a goofy face while changing a diaper yesterday and I chuckled—but it doesn’t feel as bright or lasting as it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do look forward to little things—like taking the baby for a walk to the park—but the excitement feels kind of muted. It’s more “that’ll be nice” than “I can’t wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah—like yesterday when she wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong. I know it’s probably normal baby stuff, but I still catch myself feeling like I should’ve figured it out already.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A couple of times I’ll suddenly feel my heart race, mostly when the baby’s asleep and I’m watching her breathe—then I imagine something going wrong even though she’s fine. It passes pretty quickly, but it pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full panic, but once or twice this week I got that sudden tight-chest feeling, like when I heard her cough in her sleep. It lasted maybe a minute and then I could breathe again, but it startled me.
Things have been getting on top of me
Some days, yeah—like when she wouldn’t settle and the laundry piled up, I felt as if everything was stacked too high. I still manage, but it feels heavier than it used to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say “so unhappy,” but a couple of nights I’ve lain there running through the day in my head—worrying if I burped her right, if she ate enough—and it took maybe an extra half-hour to drift off. My sleep’s mostly okay, just those moments.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel a bit down some days—like yesterday evening when everyone else seemed excited about the photos we took, and I just felt kind of empty. It’s not all day, but it’s there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yeah, I’ve cried a couple of times—once when she wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch for hours. It wasn’t sobbing, just tears that slipped out while I stared at the wall.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt tired or overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-style responses):

<sym>Low mood / anhedonia</sym>  
- Diminished pleasure/enjoyment in ordinarily pleasant activities (laughter, outings).  
- Intermittent “empty” or “muted” emotional tone.

<sym>Excessive guilt / self-blame</sym>  
- Attributions of maternal “failure” when infant routines falter.

<sym>Anxiety symptoms</sym>  
- Episodic, non-triggered racing heart, chest tightness, intrusive worries about infant safety.  
- No discrete panic attacks; brief surges of physiological arousal.

<sym>Feeling overwhelmed / coping strain</sym>  
- Reports tasks “stacked too high,” heavier perceived load than pre-baby.

<sym>Sleep disturbance mood-related</sym>  
- Occasional prolonged sleep-latency secondary to rumination; overall sleep pattern largely preserved.

<sym>Crying spells</sym>  
- Two instances of tearfulness linked to feeding/role frustration.

<sym>Self-harm ideation</sym>  
- Denied; no safety concern identified.

Pattern:  
Mild–moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms localized to postpartum period; no functional incapacitation described; no psychotic or suicidal content.

Screening significance:  
Positive indicators for <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety</med>; score suggests benefit from formal clinical interview and monitoring for symptom progression.
